raw_case_text:
Written consent was obtained from the patient for the publication of his case and images. A 66-year-old Indian male patient presented to the Tuberculosis Control Unit after sudden onset of near syncope, nausea, diaphoresis, light-headedness, and a wide-staring gaze with upward and lateral deviation of eyes 30 minutes after consuming newly-prescribed RHEZ. These symptoms resolved on the administration of diphenhydramine 25 mg intravenously at the Emergency Department. The patient was referred, initially, to the Department of Rheumatology, Allergy and Immunology based on the suspicion of a reaction to RHEZ. A diagnosis of anaphylaxis-like and possibly idiosyncratic reaction to rifampicin was made.
On further questioning by the primary team, the patient reported that while he was aware of his surroundings and was able to hear conversations around him, he felt "physical blocked" in that he was unable to respond with purposeful voluntary movements or speech; he additionally described abdominal discomfort and generalized weakness.
The patient had just been prescribed daily rifampicin 600 mg, isoniazid 300 mg, ethambutol 1.6 g, pyrazinamide 1.75 g (i.e., standard RHEZ combination therapy for TB of uncertain origin and resistance, according to his weight of 98.3 kg) and pyridoxine 10 mg after increased nodular opacities in the left upper zone were observed on sequential chest X-rays (Figures 1 and 2), suggestive of granulomata. A small calcified pleural plaque was also noted. Blood cultures, sputum cultures, and Mycobacterium tuberculosis polymerase chain reaction were negative.
On his initial presentation after the near syncope, the patient's vitals were stable and physical examination, including neurological examination, did not reveal any conclusive findings. A full blood count, liver function test, thyroid function test, drug screen, troponin I, electrocardiogram (Figure 3), and a two-dimensional echocardiography were performed.
However, the diagnosis was subsequently changed to OGC based on the more complete history recorded. Another possible cause of OGC would include trauma. However, the patient did not suffer from any trauma recently.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 66-year-old male presented with sudden-onset near-syncope, diaphoresis, light-headedness, nausea, and upward-lateral eye deviation 30 minutes after taking his first dose of antituberculous therapy.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: A 66-year-old male with presumptive pulmonary tuberculosis presented to the Tuberculosis Control Unit and emergency department 30 minutes after ingesting his newly prescribed RHEZ regimen. He developed acute light-headedness, near-syncope, diaphoresis, nausea, abdominal discomfort, generalized weakness, and fixed upward and lateral deviation of his eyes. While fully aware of his surroundings, he felt completely unable to move voluntarily or speak. Symptoms resolved promptly upon intravenous diphenhydramine administration.
subjective.past_medical_history: Body weight 98.3 kg. Prescribed daily rifampicin 600 mg, isoniazid 300 mg, ethambutol 1.6 g, pyrazinamide 1.75 g, and pyridoxine 10 mg based on sequential chest radiographs showing progressive nodular opacities. Denied recent trauma. No other medical history documented.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for near-syncope, light-headedness, diaphoresis, nausea, abdominal discomfort, generalized weakness, and inability to speak or initiate voluntary movement despite clear sensorium. Allergies not documented.

objective.physical_examination: Hemodynamically stable. Physical and neurological examinations following symptom resolution were non-focal. Initial presentation exhibited wide-staring gaze with upward and lateral eye deviation (oculogyric crisis).
objective.routine_investigations: Sequential chest X-rays: increasing nodular opacities in left upper zone consistent with granulomata, with a small calcified pleural plaque. Complete blood count, liver function tests, thyroid function tests, troponin I, and urine drug screen normal. Electrocardiogram and 2D echocardiography normal. Blood cultures, sputum cultures, and molecular pathogen testing were negative.
objective.advanced_workup: Diagnostic and therapeutic challenge: administration of intravenous diphenhydramine (25 mg) in the emergency department resulted in immediate and complete resolution of acute ocular deviation and involuntary motor block.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Definitive diagnosis: Drug-induced oculogyric crisis (OGC) and acute dystonic reaction secondary to antituberculous therapy (presumed idiosyncratic reaction to rifampicin or combination RHEZ), occurring in a patient treated for presumptive pulmonary tuberculosis. Initial suspicion of anaphylactoid reaction was revised to acute dystonia based on complete history and rapid response to anticholinergic therapy. Sputum and blood cultures and Mycobacterium tuberculosis PCR were negative. Management & Outcome: Successfully treated with intravenous diphenhydramine 25 mg with complete abortion of the crisis. Re-evaluated by rheumatology/allergy and infectious disease teams for medication adjustment.
